questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
We identify the leading term and compute its limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(4{x}^{2}-5x+16) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(4{x}^{2}) \\  & =4\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{2}) \\  & =\infty \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Odd Power
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13939873/assets/67dc6176a774b0dcb803a8e0935e2cc7c4241f635b18b7466fc530da8320cfe0.png)

The figure shows the graph of $y=f(x).$ Calculate ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{(xf(x))}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the power rule and the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{(xf(x))}^{3} & =({lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3})\cdot ({lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x)^{3}) \\  & =({lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3})\cdot {({lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x))}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x)=3.$ Therefore, the above becomes:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{(xf(x))}^{3} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {(3)}^{3} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot 27 \\  & =27\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{3}$ is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3}=-\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $27$ does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}27\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{(xf(x))}^{3}=-\infty .
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
We identify the leading term and compute its limit. In this case, we raise the main term of the base polynomial to the given power.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }({t}^{2}+1)^{4} & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }({t}^{2})^{4} \\  & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{8} \\  & =\infty \end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Constant Function
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's calculate ${x}^{2}\cdot p(x):$

$$
{x}^{2}\cdot p(x)={x}^{2}\cdot (-3{x}^{5})=-3{x}^{7}
$$

When we multiply the two functions ${x}^{2}\cdot p(x)$ and $q(x)$, we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{2}\cdot p(x)\cdot q(x)) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(-3{x}^{7}\cdot \frac{4}{{x}^{7}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }-12 \\  & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Constant Function
questions.worked_solution:
When we divide the two functions, we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(11{x}^{4})}{(5{x}^{4})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{11}{5} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}\end{aligned}
$$
